491.event_title: Hannibal encircles the Roman army at Cannae
491.event: In the Second Punic War a Roman army of more than 80,000 men under the consuls Lucius Aemilius Paullus and Gaius Terentius Varro met Hannibal's smaller Carthaginian army of under 50,000 near the river Aufidus. Hannibal placed his line in a forward-curving crescent with cavalry on the wings, and as his centre gave way the Romans pressed into it. His infantry then closed on their flanks and his cavalry came round behind them, surrounding the Roman army and destroying it.
491.explanation: Cannae became the classic example of encirclement, studied by commanders for more than two thousand years.
491.tie_back: The kural warns against engaging an enemy before finding ground from which one can surround him, and Hannibal fought only where his formation could close around the larger Roman army.
491._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of choosing ground and position for encirclement, though Hannibal's victory owed as much to his formation as to the terrain.

492.event_title: Constantinople's walls withstand the Arab siege of 717-718
492.event: Soon after Leo III became Byzantine emperor in 717, a large Umayyad army and fleet laid siege to Constantinople, which was protected by the massive Theodosian land walls and by sea walls. Behind these fortifications, and using the incendiary weapon known as Greek fire against the enemy fleet, the defenders held out through a harsh winter while the besiegers suffered from hunger and disease. With a Bulgar force also attacking them, the Arab army withdrew in August 718.
492.explanation: The victory checked the Arab advance into southeastern Europe and showed how a fortified capital multiplied the strength of its defenders.
492.tie_back: The kural says that even those already strong in war gain many advantages from a secure fortified position, and Leo's forces held on because they fought from behind Constantinople's walls.
492._accuracy_note: A reasonable illustration of a fortress adding to a defender's strength, though winter, Greek fire and Bulgar help also shaped the outcome.

493.event_title: The Swiss confederates defeat the Habsburg army at Morgarten
493.event: Duke Leopold I of Habsburg led an army of knights to invade the valley of Schwyz, marching by a narrow route between the shore of Lake Ageri and the steep slopes of Morgarten. The men of Schwyz, joined by fighters from Uri, waited on the heights and attacked the column while it was strung out in the narrow ground. Leopold's army was routed and he escaped, and the confederates renewed their alliance in the Pact of Brunnen less than a month later.
493.explanation: The victory helped secure the survival of the young Swiss confederation and gave the Swiss a lasting reputation as formidable foot soldiers.
493.tie_back: The kural says even the weak can defeat their enemies if they choose the right place and keep themselves safe, and the confederates struck from the heights where the knights could not use their strength.
493._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of the weaker side winning by choice of ground, though the Swiss National Museum notes that reliable details of the fighting are scarce.

494.event_title: Masséna halts before the Lines of Torres Vedras
494.event: During the Peninsular War, Wellington had a great network of forts, redoubts and barriers built across the hills north of Lisbon, using the natural terrain and blocking the roads, and laid waste the country in front of them. In October 1810 his Anglo-Portuguese army withdrew behind these Lines, and Marshal Masséna's French army, arriving before them, did not attempt a full assault. After a winter of great hardship and heavy losses from hunger, the French began to retreat from Portugal in March 1811.
494.explanation: Without a major battle, a well-chosen and fortified position defeated an invasion simply by making the enemy's plan impossible.
494.tie_back: The kural says that if those who have found the right place hold fast to it, enemies who planned to beat them will have to give up their plans, which is exactly what Masséna did.
494._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural: holding the right ground made the enemy abandon its purpose without a decisive battle.

495.event_title: Tran Hung Dao destroys the Mongol fleet at the Bach Dang River
495.place: Bach Dang River, near Haiphong, Vietnam
495.event: During the third Mongol invasion of Dai Viet, the Vietnamese commander Tran Hung Dao avoided pitched battles on land and then chose to fight the withdrawing Yuan fleet on the Bach Dang River. His men drove stakes into the riverbed below the waterline, a tactic used at the same river in 938, and lured the Mongol ships onto them. The fleet was wrecked and destroyed, and the invasion ended in defeat.
495.explanation: The Mongols, nearly unbeatable on the open plains, were defeated on a tidal river whose conditions their enemy understood far better.
495.tie_back: The kural's crocodile is master only in its own element, and the Mongols, masters of land warfare, were overcome once they fought on Vietnamese waters.
495._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of a power defeated outside its element, though numbers and some details of the battle vary between accounts.

496.event_title: Napoleon's Army of England waits at Boulogne
496.event: After war with Britain resumed in 1803, Napoleon gathered more than 150,000 soldiers in camps along the Channel coast around Boulogne and had well over a thousand flat-bottomed boats and barges built to carry them to England. The crossing depended on gaining control of the Channel, but the Royal Navy kept the French fleets away and the invasion never took place. In late August 1805 Napoleon marched the army east against Austria, and on 21 October 1805 the French and Spanish fleet was defeated at Trafalgar.
496.explanation: The finest land army in Europe could not reach an island enemy that ruled the sea, and Napoleon had to seek his victories on the Continent instead.
496.tie_back: The kural says a strong chariot cannot run on the sea and a ship cannot run on land, and Napoleon's Grande Armee, unbeatable on land, never crossed twenty miles of water.
496._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of land power stopped by the sea, though some historians debate how seriously Napoleon meant to invade.

497.event_title: Admiral Yi Sun-sin's stand at the Myeongnyang Strait
497.event: During Japan's second invasion of Korea, Admiral Yi Sun-sin, recently restored to command after being demoted, had only about thirteen warships left against a Japanese fleet of more than a hundred and thirty. He chose to fight in the narrow Myeongnyang Strait, whose name means roaring currents, where the channel and fast tidal flow kept many ships from passing at once. The Japanese ships were hampered and fell into confusion, and the Japanese fleet withdrew after heavy losses.
497.explanation: Careful choice of a battleground that neutralised enemy numbers allowed a tiny fleet to turn back a large one.
497.tie_back: The kural says that one who thinks everything through and acts from the right place needs no ally but fearlessness, and Yi had no allies, only his plan, the strait and his courage.
497._accuracy_note: Close to a dramatisation of the kural, though sources differ on the exact numbers of ships involved.

498.event_title: Henry V's smaller army wins at Agincourt
498.event: Henry V's English army, much smaller than the French force facing it, took position on a recently ploughed field bounded by woods on both sides, which narrowed the front. The English archers drove sharpened stakes into the ground before them, and days of rain had turned the field to deep mud. The heavily armoured French men-at-arms, advancing through the mud and crowded together in the narrow space, lost their advantage of numbers and suffered a disastrous defeat.
498.explanation: Agincourt is a classic case of a small army choosing ground where the enemy's greater numbers became a burden rather than a strength.
498.tie_back: The kural says that if a commander with a small army stands on ground where his strength prevails, the commander of a large army loses his drive and advantage, as the French did at Agincourt.
498._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural's contrast between a small force on favourable ground and a large force robbed of its advantage.

499.event_title: Ethiopia defeats the Italian invasion at Adwa
499.event: After Italy claimed Ethiopia as a protectorate, Emperor Menelik II led a large army north to meet the Italian forces advancing from Eritrea. Italian commander Oreste Baratieri ordered a night march into the mountainous country around Adwa, but his brigades became separated in the unfamiliar terrain, and Menelik's forces defeated them one after another. Italy recognised Ethiopia's full independence in the peace that followed.
499.explanation: Adwa was the first decisive defeat of a European colonial army by an African state and kept Ethiopia independent.
499.tie_back: The kural warns that people are hard to defeat when you attack them in the land where they live, and the invaders lost their way and the battle in Ethiopia's own mountains.
499._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit for the home-ground advantage, but the kural speaks of defenders without special strength, while Menelik's army was large and well armed.

500.event_title: Flemish townsmen defeat the French knights at the Battle of the Golden Spurs
500.event: When the towns of Flanders rose against French rule, a French army of professional mounted knights was sent against them. The Flemish army, made up largely of townspeople and craft guildsmen fighting on foot, took a stand on ground bounded by streams and ditches, where marshy soil hampered the horsemen. The French cavalry charge broke down on this ground and the knights were defeated by the foot soldiers, who afterwards collected the fallen knights' spurs as trophies.
500.explanation: The battle showed that the most prestigious troops of the age could be beaten by ordinary infantry once they were caught on ground that suited the defender.
500.tie_back: The kural says the fearless war elephant can be killed even by jackals once it is stuck in mud, and the proud French knights were brought down by humble townsmen in the marshes of Courtrai.
500._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural: the mightiest arm of war, caught in mire, defeated by those it despised.
